items.statement: Earwigs crawl into people's ears.
items.explanation: It's a very old tale. Earwigs look for dark, damp spots under rocks and leaves; their pincers are for defense, and our ears don't interest them.

items.statement: A big black moth that flies into the house brings bad luck.
items.explanation: It's the black witch moth. It flies at night and comes in looking for a dark place to rest. It doesn't bring bad luck: it's harmless and is food for bats and birds.

items.statement: Spiders are insects.
items.explanation: Spiders have eight legs, two body parts and no antennae: they're arachnids, cousins of insects.

items.statement: Almost all spiders are harmless to people.
items.explanation: Their venom is for hunting insects and is almost always very weak for us. The few dangerous ones, and any you don't know, are watched from a distance.

items.statement: A centipede has exactly one hundred legs.
items.explanation: Depending on the species it has from 30 to more than 300 legs, but never exactly one hundred. Its name just means “lots of legs.”

items.statement: Only female mosquitoes bite.
items.explanation: Females need blood for their eggs to grow. Males only drink nectar from flowers.

items.statement: A ladybug's spots tell you how old it is.
items.explanation: The spots depend on the kind of ladybug, not its age. There are ladybugs with 2 spots, with 7 and even with none! Most live about a year.

items.statement: Crickets sing with their mouths.
items.explanation: Crickets sing by rubbing one wing against the other, like a violin bow. And they hear with ears on their front legs!

items.statement: Flies taste food with their feet.
items.explanation: Their feet have tiny hairs that sense taste. So when they land, they already know if something is food. That's why it's good to cover food.

items.statement: Dragonflies sting people.
items.explanation: Dragonflies have no stinger and don't hurt people. Quite the opposite: they catch mosquitoes in midair!

items.statement: Leafcutter ants eat the leaves they cut.
items.explanation: They use the leaves to feed a fungus garden inside the nest, and what they eat is the fungus. They're farmers!

items.statement: Scorpions glow under ultraviolet light.
items.explanation: Their shell has something that glows blue-green under that light. Scientists find them that way at night, without touching them.

items.statement: The blue morpho is blue because its wings have blue pigment.
items.explanation: Its scales have tiny shapes that reflect blue light, like a soap bubble. That's why it shimmers and changes depending on where you look from.

items.statement: A honeybee usually dies if it stings a person.
items.explanation: Its stinger has tiny hooks and gets stuck in our skin. That's why it only stings when it really feels in danger.

items.statement: Some bees don't sting.
items.explanation: The angelita bee and its cousins are stingless bees: their stinger is so tiny it doesn't work. They defend their nest by tangling in hair and nibbling.

items.statement: A click beetle firefly gets burned by its own light.
items.explanation: It's a cold light: almost all the energy becomes light and almost none becomes heat. That's why its lanterns don't burn it.

items.statement: All cockroaches live in houses and are pests.
items.explanation: There are thousands of kinds, and almost all live in the forest recycling leaves. Only a few come into houses looking for food.

items.statement: If you touch a butterfly's wings, it dies instantly.
items.explanation: It doesn't die instantly, but it does lose the dust on its wings, which are scales that never grow back. That's why it's better to look without touching.

items.statement: Wasps are useless.
items.explanation: Wasps hunt caterpillars and other pests, and some help flowers make seeds. Without them, gardens would have many more pests.

items.statement: An ant can carry several times its own weight.
items.explanation: Depending on the species, an ant can carry 10 to 50 times its weight. Like you lifting a car!
